theme: Balaam, God’s sovereignty over a false prophet
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 22:1-24:25. This is the story of Balaam, the prophet hired to curse Israel who can only bless them. It is full of irony and humor, and also one of the most important prophecies of the Messiah in the Old Testament. Notice who sees what.
settingTheScene: Israel has camped on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, opposite Jericho. Balak, the king of Moab, is afraid of them. He hires Balaam, a diviner from Mesopotamia, to curse Israel. God will not let him. Balaam goes, and three times he tries to curse, and three times he blesses. The story is told from a distance. Israel never hears of it, but God is fighting for them without their knowledge.
observation: Balak says, “He whom you bless is blessed, and he whom you curse is cursed” (22:6).
God tells Balaam, “You shall not go with them. You shall not curse the people, for they are blessed” (22:12).
Balaam goes with Balak’s men, and the donkey sees the angel of the LORD three times before Balaam does (22:21-35).
The donkey speaks: “What have I done to you, that you have struck me these three times?” (22:28).
Balaam says, “I cannot go beyond the command of the LORD my God to do less or more” (22:18).
“God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (23:19).
“He has not beheld misfortune in Jacob, nor has he seen trouble in Israel. The LORD their God is with them” (23:21).
“I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near: a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel” (24:17).
interpretation:
The story of Balaam is comic and serious at the same time. A prophet-for-hire, who is hoping for a large payment, is outwitted by his own donkey. The animal sees the angel of the LORD, and the professional seer does not. He is more eager for money than for truth. The irony is complete when the donkey speaks and Balaam answers it as though it were normal to argue with a donkey.

The deeper point is that no one can curse those whom God has blessed. Balak thinks that the right words, from the right person, in the right place, can turn God’s favor away. But God’s blessing is not a thing to be manipulated. “How can I curse whom God has not cursed?” (23:8). The blessing was given in the covenant with Abraham, and it will not be undone by any spell.

The oracle in 23:19 is among the clearest statements of God’s faithfulness: “God is not man, that he should lie.” He does not change his mind the way people do. When he promises, he does it. The people do not know any of this is happening, which is the beauty of it. While Israel sleeps in their tents, God defends them.

The last oracle, in 24:17, is the high point. Balaam, who came to curse, ends by announcing a coming king: “a star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel.” It looks ahead to David, who crushed Moab, and beyond David to the final King. The oracle is spoken by a pagan prophet, whose own heart is not changed. God can use anyone to speak his word, even one who does not love him.

The tragedy of Balaam is that he knew all this and still ended badly. In the next chapter, you will see how Balaam’s counsel led Israel into sin.
connection: The magi who followed a star to Bethlehem (Matthew 2:2) probably knew this prophecy. Jesus is called “the bright morning star” in Revelation 22:16. Paul says that “if God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31), and “nothing… will be able to separate us from the love of God” (Romans 8:38-39). Peter and Jude warn about the way of Balaam, which loves gain from wrongdoing (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11).
application:
Remember that no curse can undo what God has blessed in Christ. Take comfort in that if you are afraid.

Ask whether you are ever more concerned with reward than with truth, like Balaam.

Thank God that he fights for you even when you are unaware of it.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that those he has blessed cannot be cursed.
Thank him for the Star who came out of Jacob.
Ask him to keep you from loving gain more than truth.
